newsitem.title: CANADA: Proposed Canada-U.S. gas pipeline courts producers.
newsitem.headline: Proposed Canada-U.S. gas pipeline courts producers.

text.p: The backers of a newly proposed US$1-billion natural gas pipeline to the U.S. Midwest from Canada took their pitch to Canadian producers on Thursday in hopes of winning support for the latest in a string of competing projects.

The Viking Voyageur Gas Transmission project, proposed by Northern States Power Co unit Viking Gas Transmission and TransCanada PipeLines Ltd, would move gas to markets in Minnesota, Wisconsin and Illinois from southern Manitoba.

The project owners and a group of local distribution company representatives from the states held an open house in Calgary to explain the the benefits to producers of direct access to markets in Minneapolis, Madison, Milwaukee and Chicago by late 1999.

The 800 mile Viking Voyaguer line would ship 1.2 billion cubic feet of gas per day to LDCs in those cities, which -- with the exception of Chicago -- have little choice of pipelines to secure supply. The result has been far higher city gate prices than those in more southerly Midwest markets, proponents said.

Four Wisconsin utilities, which have banded together to form the Wisconsin Capacity Coalition, have thrown their support behind the project and pledged to spend about US$160 million on lateral lines, meter and regulator stations and system enhnacements to hook their systems up to Viking Voyageur.

The LDCs include Madison Gas & Electric Co, Wisconsin Fuel & Light Co, Wisconsin Gas Co and Wisconsin Public Service Corp, which together buy about 233 billion cubic feet of gas per year out of a state total of 376 BCF per year.
In Minnesota, Viking Voyageur has the support of Northern States and NorAm Energy Corp unit Minnegasco.
Under the proposal, the line would follow the existing Viking Gas right-of-way to Marshfield, Wisconsin from Emerson, Manitoba. From there, new pipeline would be added to Joliet, Illinois.
Canadian producers have also been hampered by a lack of export pipeline space. For them, it has resulted in far lower prices than those received by their U.S. counterparts.

Viking Voyageur officials said the line would offer a "postage stamp" toll of 39 cents per million British thermal units for any destination along the line, allowing lower tolls than by moving volumes through several pipes.
They said the line would offer benefits that the proposed 1.3 billion cubic feet a day Alliance Pipeline, a partnership of several Canadian Energy firms, could not.
One was the availablity to access the upper Midwest market, which players said was suffering with a lack of pipeline competition.
the C$3.6 billion ($2.6 billion) Alliance line would extend directly to Chicago from northeast British Columbia.
Viking Voyageur is one of several pipeline projects recently prposed to cure Canada's shortage of gas export capacity.
An open season to gain shipper support for the project would likely start in early may, company officials said.
